entry.title: Week 9: The RAM model
entry.content:
Week 9 · 30 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Moving past Turing machines to a computation model closer to real hardware.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B3: the RAM (Random Access Machine) model and worked examples. B3-1 covered the model itself, B3-2 applied it to concrete problems. Also finished the 01B 计算模型 assignment and watched the video explanation for it.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

The jump from Turing machines to RAM felt big at first. A Turing machine reads one cell at a time and shuffles left or right. A RAM can reach any memory address in one step. In the Turing model, just reading the input is already O(n) because each cell takes a step to reach. In the RAM model, memory access, comparison, and arithmetic all cost O(1), so you count how many of those operations your code uses.

I followed the B3-2 examples along with the lecture, pausing to count the operations myself before the video showed the answer.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I reviewed my B2 notes before starting so the comparison made sense, and I finished the 01B assignment on my own before watching the explanation video.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Start using the RAM model to estimate costs of simple code I write, so the counting becomes automatic.

Evidence

XuetangX watch history for B3-1 and B3-2. Completed 01B 计算模型 assignment and its video explanation.

entry.title: Week 7: Where I've actually got to
entry.content:

Checkpoint session. Built this website and reviewed my progress so far.

1. What I worked on

Set up this site (Hexo + Fluid theme on GitHub Pages) and mapped out what I’ve covered across five sessions.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Stepping back from the course content to take stock. It’s easy to keep watching the next video, so I used this session to review what I’ve covered so far: course selection, computation theory, Turing machines. Seeing the whole thing laid out made the progression through Chapter 1 clearer than it felt week by week. Setting up the site meant choosing a structure that’s easy to maintain: journal entries by week, a resources page, and a learner bio placeholder for Semester 2.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I decided to build this site and do a checkpoint review without being asked. Nobody assigned this; I wanted to see where I am before the semester goes further.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Start submitting to the online judge. The next topics (RAM model, big-O) should have code exercises. Also keep up the routine of reviewing notes before each Friday.

entry.title: Week 5: Turing machines
entry.content:
Week 5 · 2 October 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Back after a two-week gap. Mid-Autumn Festival meant no class on the 25th.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B2: the Turing machine model and a worked example. Two videos, then I traced the example on paper myself.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Tracing the B2-2 example: I was reading the transition table top-to-bottom like code, but it’s actually a lookup table. You find your (state, character) pair and read off what to do. Once I figured that out the rest of the trace went fine. I also spent the first few minutes reviewing week 3 notes so I didn’t start cold after the break.

The bigger question, why study Turing machines at all, clicked by the end. It defines what “computable” means, which matters when the course starts asking whether a problem is even solvable.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I traced the example on paper, caught my own mistake with the transition table, and reviewed previous notes before starting. Also looked ahead at what’s next (RAM model, big-O) to have context.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Keep reviewing previous notes before each session. It made a clear difference today.

Evidence

Paper trace of the B2-2 Turing machine example.

entry.title: Week 3: How you measure an algorithm
entry.content:
Week 3 · 18 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

All theory this week. Measuring algorithms without running them.

1. What I worked on

绪论 B1: performance measurement, problem size, worst-case analysis, and the idealised computation model.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Writing cost as T(n) instead of a single number was new. For sorting, n is the array length; for multiplication, n is the digit count. Same letter, totally different meaning. I paused the video and worked through my own examples until it felt natural. Worst-case analysis I already knew from competitive programming (you always check the worst input), but the course treats it as a modelling choice, not just common sense. That reframe was useful.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I kept connecting the theory to stuff I already knew from competitive programming, which helped the abstract parts make sense. I paused videos to think through things on my own.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

After each video, close the tab and restate the main idea in one sentence before moving on.

Evidence

Notes on T(n), worst-case vs average-case, and the idealised model.

entry.title: Week 2: Setting up, and what computation means
entry.content:
Week 2 · 11 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

Got everything set up and started the first real lectures.

1. What I worked on

Enrolled on XuetangX, registered on the Tsinghua OJ, set up g++ locally. Then watched 绪论 A on what “computation” means: rope computers, straightedge constructions, the four properties of an algorithm.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

I expected code and got geometry. The rope and straightedge examples seemed random, but they’re about what counts as a “basic operation” in different models. You can’t analyse an algorithm until you agree what one step is. The four algorithm properties (correctness, determinism, feasibility, finiteness) gave me trouble too. I kept mixing up feasibility and finiteness until the Hailstone sequence example made it click. A program that might run forever isn’t an algorithm, even if every step is simple.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I stuck with the parts that seemed pointless instead of skipping ahead, and they turned out to matter. Also caught the OJ same-email requirement by reading the docs before registering.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Do all setup outside of class so the full period goes to content.

Evidence

Registered on XuetangX and the OJ. Notes on the four algorithm properties and Hailstone.

entry.title: Week 1: Picking the course took longer than I thought it would
entry.content:
Week 1 · 4 September 2026 · Data Structures (数据结构), Tsinghua University · XuetangX

First session. Spent it choosing which course to take for VLD.

1. What I worked on

Compared four courses and picked Tsinghua’s Data Structures (数据结构) by Prof. Deng Junhui on XuetangX. Also checked the prerequisites and found the online judge for assignments.

2. What was challenging, and how I handled it

Every option had a trade-off. Stanford CS106B has no grading, UC San Diego mixes three languages, UIUC is too short for a full year. I kept going back and forth until I wrote down three criteria (graded work, C++ only, free), and only Tsinghua hit all three. Once I knew what I was comparing on, the decision was obvious.

3. How well I ran my own learning

Self-score: 100

I picked my own criteria and chose the course myself. The comparison was my idea, not something I was told to do.

4. What I’ll do differently next session

Enrol on XuetangX and register on the OJ in one go. The OJ account needs the same email as XuetangX for grades to sync.

Evidence

Course comparison and all links on my Resources page.
